questions.title: Difference between 'intrinsic evidence' and 'propensity evidence' under FRE 404(b) in firearm possession cases
questions.question_body: I'm reading United States v. Cutbank, and the defendant argued that testifying about him possessing a gun *before* the crime was propensity evidence (Rule 404(b)). However, the court called it 'intrinsic evidence' to prove possession. I'm confused—isn't showing he had a gun in the past just showing he has a 'propensity' to possess guns? Why does the court treat prior possession as a direct element of the current charge rather than character evidence?

questions.title: Timing of limiting instructions and the Confrontation Clause
questions.question_body: In this case, the defendant wanted the jury to be instructed *immediately* that police testimony about a victim's statements shouldn't be used as substantive evidence until the victim actually testified. The court said a limiting instruction at the end of the trial is sufficient. Is it standard practice to wait until the end of the trial to give these instructions, and does this not risk the jury 'poisoning' their view of the defendant before the actual testimony is heard?

questions.title: Authentication requirements for using police reports as extrinsic evidence for impeachment
questions.question_body: The court ruled that the defense couldn't read portions of a police report into the record to impeach a witness because the report wasn't authored by the witness (lack of authentication). I thought that for impeachment purposes, the goal is just to show a prior inconsistent statement. If the witness admits they spoke to the police, why is a formal authentication of the police report still required before the specific words can be read?

questions.title: Applying USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) for 'uncharged' felony offenses
questions.question_body: The court applied a 4-level sentencing enhancement because the firearm was used 'in connection with another felony offense,' even though the opinion implies the defendant wasn't necessarily convicted of that separate felony. How can a court enhance a sentence based on the commission of a felony if there was no separate charge or conviction for that specific act? Is the burden of proof for this enhancement lower than 'beyond a reasonable doubt'?

questions.title: Interaction between ACCA Guidelines and General Guidelines offense levels
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the sentencing math in this opinion. It says the ACCA Guideline would have resulted in an offense level of 34, but because of other enhancements (like the sawed-off barrel and altered serial number), the total offense level was 35. The court then says 'the greater offense level applies.' Is it my understanding that if a defendant is an Armed Career Criminal, the ACCA guidelines usually override everything else, or do they just act as a 'floor' that can be increased by other specific offense characteristics?

questions.title: Rule 403 analysis: When does personal tragedy become 'unfair prejudice'?
questions.question_body: During cross-examination, a witness mentioned her sister was killed by a gun to explain why she was unfamiliar with firearms. The defendant tried to strike this under Rule 403. Usually, mentions of death or violence are seen as highly prejudicial. Why did the court find this specific piece of testimony acceptable rather than 'unfairly prejudicial' to the defendant?
